q: Who is known as the Father of Genetics?
e: Gregor Johann Mendel formulated the fundamental laws of inheritance using garden pea experiments.

q: Which plant did Mendel choose for his experiments on heredity?
e: Mendel chose the garden pea because it had distinct contrasting traits, short life cycle and easy self/cross pollination.

q: How many chromosomes are present in normal human body cells? (JAC 2020)
e: Humans possess 46 chromosomes (23 pairs)—22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes.

q: What are the sex chromosomes in human males and females respectively?
e: Human females have a perfect pair XX, whereas males have a mismatched pair XY.

q: Who proposed the theory of evolution by Natural Selection? (JAC 2025)
e: Charles Darwin proposed the theory of evolution of species by natural selection.

q: Sex of a human child is determined by:
o: Whether the father's sperm contributes an X or Y chromosome
e: All eggs carry X, whereas sperms carry either X or Y; hence the chromosome inherited from the father determines the child's sex.

q: In Mendel's monohybrid cross between pure tall (TT) and pure short (tt) pea plants, all F₁ plants were:
e: Because tallness (T) is dominant over shortness (t), all F₁ heterozygous (Tt) plants were tall.

q: What is the phenotypic ratio (Tall : Short) in the F₂ generation of Mendel's monohybrid cross?
e: Selfing F₁ (Tt × Tt) produces 3 tall (TT, Tt, Tt) and 1 short (tt) plant, giving a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio.

q: What is the genotypic ratio (TT : Tt : tt) in the F₂ generation of a monohybrid cross?
e: The F₂ genotypic ratio of TT : Tt : tt is 1 : 2 : 1.

q: In a cross between pure tall (TT) and pure short (tt) pea plants, what is the ratio of PURE tall plants to PURE short plants in the F₂ generation? (JAC 2026)
e: Note carefully: F₂ genotypes are TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1. Therefore the ratio of PURE tall (TT) to PURE short (tt) is 1 : 1!

q: What is the F₂ phenotypic ratio obtained in Mendel's dihybrid cross?
e: Independent assortment of two traits yields a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio in F₂.

q: In evolutionary terms, we have more in common with: (NCERT)
e: All humans worldwide belong to the exact same species (Homo sapiens), so a Chinese school-boy has far more in common with us than any other species.

q: What do homologous organs indicate? (JAC 2020)
o: Common evolutionary ancestor (same basic structure/origin, different functions)
e: Forelimbs of frog, lizard, bird and human share the same basic skeletal design for different functions, showing common ancestry.

q: Which of the following is an example of homologous organs? (NCERT)
o: Our arm and a dog's fore-leg (or our teeth and an elephant's tusks)
e: Our arm and a dog's foreleg share basic vertebrate limb anatomy (homologous), unlike bird and butterfly wings (analogous).

q: Organs having different basic structural origin/design but performing the same function (e.g., wings of bat/bird and wings of insect) are called:
e: Wings of insects and birds/bats have totally different structural origins yet both are adapted for flying—these are analogous organs.

q: Which of the following is an ACQUIRED trait (non-inherited)? (JAC 2025)
o: Size/weight of the body or learning to swim
e: Body size/weight changes due to nutrition or exercise affect somatic tissues only, not germ-cell DNA, so they are acquired traits.

q: A section of DNA that provides information for one specific protein is called:
e: A section of DNA carrying information to synthesise a particular protein is called a gene for that protein.

q: Who suggested that life must have developed from simple inorganic molecules present on early Earth?
e: J.B.S. Haldane suggested in 1929 that life originated from simple inorganic molecules, later tested experimentally by Miller and Urey.

q: Preserved traces or remains of ancient living organisms found in rocks are called:
e: Preserved remains or impressions of ancient organisms in sedimentary rocks are called fossils.

q: According to genetic footprints and fossil evidence, where can the earliest members of Homo sapiens be traced?
e: Human genetic footprints trace all modern humans back to earliest Homo sapiens roots in Africa.

q: If the tails of a group of mice are surgically removed for several generations, will tailless mice be born?
o: No, because cutting the tail is an acquired change in somatic tissues that does not alter germ-cell DNA
e: Changes in non-reproductive tissues cannot be passed to DNA of germ cells, so offspring still inherit normal tails.

q: Which set of vegetables has been developed from Wild Cabbage by farmers over thousands of years via artificial selection?
o: Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and kale
e: Human artificial selection transformed wild cabbage into cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and kale.

q: In Mendel's notation for pea height, 'T' and 't' represent:
o: Two alternative forms (dominant and recessive versions) of the height gene
e: T (dominant version) and t (recessive version) are two alternative forms/copies of the gene controlling plant height.

q: A trait in an offspring is influenced by: (JAC 2024)
o: Both paternal and maternal DNA equally
e: Both father and mother contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material to the child, so each trait can be influenced by both DNAs.

q: The trait that expresses itself even in the heterozygous (single-copy, e.g., Tt) condition is called:
e: Since a single copy of 'T' is enough to make the plant tall (Tt), tallness is dominant and shortness (t, needing two copies tt) is recessive.

q: The process of formation of new species from an existing population is called:
e: When subpopulations become reproductively isolated over generations via drift and natural selection, new species form—called speciation.

q: Ammonite, Trilobite and Rajasaurus are famous examples of:
e: Trilobite and Ammonite are ancient marine invertebrate fossils, and Rajasaurus is a dinosaur fossil found in India's Narmada valley.

q: When Mendel crossed pea plants with round yellow seeds (RRYY) and wrinkled green seeds (rryy), what were all the F₁ seeds like?
e: Round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r) and Yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y), so all F₁ seeds were round and yellow.

q: Which flatworm possesses rudimentary light-sensitive 'eye spots' representing an early step in eye evolution?
e: Planaria has very simple 'eye spots' that merely detect light, illustrating evolution of complex organs through intermediate stages.

q: Feathers initially evolved in dinosaurs for what purpose, before later getting adapted by birds for flight?
o: For providing thermal insulation in cold weather
e: Feathers first evolved for insulation in cold climates (seen in dinosaur fossils) and were later co-opted for flight in birds.

q: In their famous 1953 experiment supporting chemical origin of life, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey took an atmosphere mimicking early Earth containing:
o: Ammonia (NH₃), methane (CH₄), hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) and water vapour (NO free O₂)
e: Using oxygen-free NH₃, CH₄, H₂S and steam with electrical sparks at <100°C, they obtained amino acids that build proteins.

q: Which two methods are used to estimate the age of fossils?
o: Relative depth method (shallower layers = recent, deeper = older) and Isotope/Radiocarbon dating (ratio of isotopes in fossil)
e: Relative stratigraphy checks rock layer depth, while fossil dating measures ratios of different isotopes of the same element (e.g. C-14).

q: In NCERT's beetle illustration, an elephant steps on a bush leaving only a few blue beetles alive purely by chance, turning the later population blue. Which evolutionary force is this?
o: Genetic drift (accidental change in small population)
e: Because survival was purely accidental with no adaptive advantage to blue colour, this random frequency shift in a small population is genetic drift.

q: Green beetles blend into green leaves and escape crows while red beetles get eaten, gradually making the whole population green. This illustrates:
e: Green colour confers a survival advantage against predators, so crows naturally select against red beetles—natural selection.

q: During a plant disease, beetles are poorly nourished and lose body weight over years; once leaves recover, new generations immediately regain normal weight. Why wasn't low weight inherited?
o: Because weight loss due to starvation is a non-genetic acquired change in non-reproductive tissues that does not alter germ-cell DNA
e: Starvation reduces body mass in somatic cells without altering DNA in germ cells, proving acquired traits are not inherited.

q: What did Mendel conclude from the appearance of new recombinant traits (Round-Green and Wrinkled-Yellow) in the F₂ generation of a dihybrid cross?
o: Round is permanently linked to yellow
Two different traits (seed shape and seed colour) are inherited independently of each other
e: Appearance of new combinations (Round-Green and Wrinkled-Yellow) proves that seed shape and seed colour assort independently.

q: In some reptiles like turtles and crocodiles, what determines the sex of the offspring developing inside the egg?
o: The temperature at which fertilised eggs are incubated
e: Unlike humans, in several reptiles the environmental temperature at which fertilised eggs are incubated determines sex.

q: Why is there an equal 50% probability of a boy or a girl in every human pregnancy?
o: Mother makes X and Y eggs
Mother always gives X; father produces 50% X-sperms (giving XX girl) and 50% Y-sperms (giving XY boy)
e: Since every egg carries X and sperms carry X or Y in equal proportions, each child has a 50% chance of inheriting X (girl) or Y (boy) from the father.

q: What special fact about sex determination in snails is noted in NCERT?
o: Snails can change sex during their lifetime, indicating sex is not genetically fixed
e: NCERT states that individuals of certain species like snails can change sex, indicating sex is not genetically determined.

q: Which pair correctly lists Dominant trait vs Recessive trait in garden pea studied by Mendel?
o: Round & Yellow seeds (Dominant) vs Wrinkled & Green seeds (Recessive)
e: In garden pea: Tall, Round seed, Yellow cotyledon and Violet flower are dominant over short, wrinkled, green seed and white flower.

q: According to NCERT, how does a gene directly control a physical characteristic like tallness in pea plants?
o: The gene codes for an enzyme synthesising a plant growth hormone; efficient enzyme yields plenty of hormone (tall), whereas altered less-efficient enzyme makes less hormone (short)
e: NCERT explains that genes control traits via proteins/enzymes: efficient enzyme produces more growth hormone (tall plant), while altered enzyme makes less (short plant).

q: If every diploid cell has two copies of each chromosome (one from mother, one from father), how many copies of each chromosome/gene enter a germ cell (gamete)?
o: Only one chromosome from each pair (single set)
e: Each germ cell takes one chromosome from each pair (either maternal or paternal) so fertilisation restores the paired diploid state.

q: How were Cauliflower and Kohlrabi respectively selected from Wild Cabbage by farmers?
o: Cauliflower was selected for sterile flowers, and Kohlrabi was selected for swollen parts
e: Sterile flowers gave cauliflower, arrested flower development gave broccoli, swollen parts gave kohlrabi, larger leaves gave kale, and short leaf spacing gave cabbage.

q: If digging deeper into undisturbed sedimentary rock strata reveals fossils in layers X (10 m deep) and Y (100 m deep), which fossil is older?
o: Fossil in deeper layer Y (100 m deep) is older
e: According to relative fossil stratigraphy, fossils found closer to the surface are more recent than those found in deeper layers.

q: When a pure Round-Yellow pea plant (RRYY) is crossed with a pure Round-Green pea plant (RRyy), what will ALL the F₁ offspring look like?
e: Both parents pass R (making all RR = round), while Y dominates y (Yy = yellow), yielding 100% Round and Yellow seeds.

q: Why should biological evolution NOT be equated with 'progress' towards a 'better' final organism?
o: Because evolution generates diversity shaped by environmental selection—not a ladder of perfection—and simplest bacteria still thrive in extreme habitats
e: Evolution is a branching generation of diversity, not a ladder of progress; ancient bacteria still survive successfully in hot springs and deep-sea vents.

q: On what principle does Molecular Phylogeny trace evolutionary relationships among organisms?
o: Comparing DNA sequence changes—more closely related species show fewer DNA differences accumulated since their common ancestor
e: Since DNA changes accumulate over time during reproduction, comparing DNA across species reveals how recently they shared a common ancestor.

q: Would geographical isolation be a major factor in the speciation of a strictly self-pollinating plant species? Why or why not?
o: No, because a self-pollinating plant already has negligible gene flow with other individuals, so a physical barrier adds no new reproductive isolation
e: NCERT Exercise Q7: Geographical isolation prevents gene flow between sexually interbreeding subpopulations; a self-pollinating plant does not cross with other plants anyway.

q: Which statement is evolutionarily accurate regarding humans and chimpanzees?
o: Humans evolved directly from modern chimpanzees
Humans and chimpanzees evolved along two separate branches from a common ancestor long ago
e: NCERT clarifies humans did not evolve from chimpanzees; rather, both shared a common ancestor and branched into separate evolutionary lines.

q: How does a recessive trait like dwarfness disappear in the F₁ generation yet reappear unchanged in F₂?
o: In F₁ (Tt), the recessive copy 't' remains intact though unexpressed; when two 't' gametes fuse in F₂ (tt), dwarfness reappears
e: Following Mendel's Law of Segregation, the recessive allele stays unblended in F₁ heterozygotes and segregates cleanly to recombine as tt in F₂.

q: Finding fish fossils in deeper rock layers and mammal fossils in shallower rock layers tells us that:
o: Fishes existed on Earth much earlier in evolutionary history than mammals
e: Deeper strata were deposited earlier in time, indicating fishes evolved earlier than mammals.

q: Which famous experiment proved that organic molecules (amino acids) could form abiotically from simple inorganic gases under early Earth conditions?
o: Stanley Miller and Harold Urey's 1953 spark-discharge experiment
e: In 1953, Miller and Urey passed electric sparks through NH₃, CH₄, H₂S and steam for a week and detected synthesis of amino acids.

q: Why are all humans classified under a single biological species (Homo sapiens) despite large differences in skin colour, height and hair?
o: Because there is no biological barrier—all humans share basic anatomy and can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
e: There is no biological basis to the notion of human 'races'; all humans share recent African ancestry and freely interbreed.

q: Are the wings of a beetle and the wings of a bat homologous or analogous organs?
e: Beetle wings are chitinous membranes while bat wings are stretched skin over elongated finger bones—different structure, same flying function, hence analogous.

q: How do the wings of a bat differ structurally from the wings of a bird?
o: Bat wings are skin folds stretched mainly between elongated fingers, whereas bird wings are feathery coverings all along the entire arm/forelimb
e: As illustrated in NCERT Fig 9.9, both use modified vertebrate forelimbs (homologous base), yet their flight surfaces evolved independently (skin membrane vs feathers).

q: If an organism has two dissimilar copies of a gene (e.g., Rr), which copy decides the expressed external trait?
e: In a heterozygous genotype (Rr), the dominant allele expresses its phenotype while the recessive allele stays masked.

q: Which parent produces two genetically different kinds of gametes with respect to sex chromosomes in humans?
e: Females are homogametic (all X eggs) whereas males are heterogametic (half X sperms, half Y sperms).

q: When two subpopulations of beetles remain separated by a huge river for hundreds of generations, what forces drive them to diverge into different species?
o: Accumulation of different random genetic drift and local natural selection in each isolated subpopulation eventually leads to reproductive isolation
e: Without gene flow, genetic drift and natural selection act differently in the two separated subpopulations until they can no longer interbreed.

q: Finding vestigial structures or tracing shared vertebrate limb skeletons belongs to studying:
e: Comparing anatomical structures across organisms reveals evolutionary relationships and common ancestry.

q: In a dihybrid cross producing 160 F₂ plants (ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1), approximately how many plants will show BOTH recessive traits (wrinkled and green seeds)?
e: Total ratio units = 9+3+3+1 = 16. Both-recessive proportion = 1/16 × 160 = 10 plants.

q: A Mendelian experiment consisted of breeding tall pea plants bearing violet flowers with short pea plants bearing white flowers. All progeny bore violet flowers, but almost half of them were short. What was the genetic make-up of the tall parent? (NCERT)
e: 100% violet flowers when crossed with ww implies the violet parent was homozygous WW. Half short progeny (Tt × tt) implies it was heterozygous Tt. Genotype: TtWW.

q: When a heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) is crossed with a pure short pea plant (tt), what is the ratio of tall to short offspring?
e: Tt produces T and t gametes; tt gives only t. Offspring are 50% Tt (tall) and 50% tt (short), giving a 1 : 1 ratio.

q: A study found that children with light-coloured eyes are likely to have parents with light-coloured eyes. On this basis, can we say anything about whether the light eye colour trait is dominant or recessive? Wait—similar NCERT Q2: A man with blood group A marries a woman with blood group O and their daughter has blood group O. Is this information enough to tell which trait (A or O) is dominant? (NCERT)
o: No, this information is NOT enough—both cases are possible unless we know the parents' genotypes or another child/parental lineage
e: NCERT Exercise Q2: By itself, this single marriage data is insufficient to prove dominance—because even if A is dominant and the father is heterozygous (Iᴬi), the daughter can still inherit 'i' from both parents to be type O.

q: In a monohybrid cross (Tt × Tt), out of 800 F₂ offspring, how many plants are expected to be heterozygous tall (Tt)?
e: In F₂ genotype ratio 1(TT) : 2(Tt) : 1(tt), heterozygous Tt forms 2/4 = 50% of 800 = 400 plants.

q: In Mendel's dihybrid cross F₂ generation (9:3:3:1) yielding 1600 seeds, how many seeds are expected to be 'Round and Green'?
e: In the 9:3:3:1 ratio, Round-Green occupies 3/16 of total offspring: (3/16) × 1600 = 300 seeds.

q: A couple already has 3 daughters. What is the probability that their fourth child will be a boy?
e: Each pregnancy is an independent event where X- or Y-bearing sperm has an equal 50% probability of fertilising the X egg.

q: If a trait A exists in 10% of a population of an asexually reproducing species and a trait B exists in 60% of the same population, which trait is likely to have arisen earlier? (NCERT)
o: Trait B, as it has been replicating over more generations and thus spread to a larger proportion (60%)
e: NCERT In-text Q1: In an asexual population, an earlier-arising neutral variation replicates over more generations to reach 60% frequency before a newer 10% trait.

q: Sweet potato is a modified root whereas potato is a modified stem, yet both are swollen underground food-storing structures. They are:
e: Different structural origins (stem vs root) performing the same function (food storage) make potato and sweet potato analogous structures.

q: Why are thorns of Bougainvillea (for protection) and tendrils of Cucurbita (for climbing) considered homologous organs?
o: Both originate from axillary buds/stems (common structural origin) but perform different functions
e: Arising from the same anatomical part (axillary bud) while serving different functions (protection vs support) defines homology.

q: Which parental cross produces 100% heterozygous tall (Tt) offspring in the next generation?
e: Homozygous TT contributes T and homozygous tt contributes t, yielding 100% Tt offspring.

q: Radioactive Carbon-14 decays steadily after an organism dies. If Fossil X retains much less C-14 ratio than Fossil Y, which fossil is older?
e: Since C-14 decays over time after death, lower remaining C-14 in Fossil X indicates it is much older than Fossil Y.

q: Can learning a foreign language or developing muscular strength during one's lifetime be genetically inherited by one's children?
o: No, because experiences in somatic tissues (brain/muscles) do not alter the DNA of germ cells
e: Only variations present in the DNA of germ cells (gametes) are inherited, not acquired somatic modifications.

q: Why could complex organs like the human eye or bird wings NOT have evolved in a single sudden DNA change?
o: Because complex organs evolve gradually across countless generations through intermediate stages, each conferring a selective survival advantage
e: NCERT explains evolution proceeds by stages where even rudimentary forms (like Planaria's eye spot or insulating feathers) provided selective benefits.

q: How many genetically different types of gametes can a dihybrid pea plant with genotype TtWw produce?
e: By independent assortment, a doubly heterozygous TtWw plant forms 4 equally likely gametes: TW, Tw, tW and tw.

q: Which factor makes evolutionary classification mirror the closeness of relationships between different species?
o: Sharing a more recent common ancestor reflected in homologous traits and minimal DNA divergence
e: The more characteristics two species share in common, the more closely related they are and the more recently they shared a common ancestor.

q: If a father has blood group AB (genotype IᴬIᴮ) and a mother has blood group O (genotype ii), what blood groups are possible in their children?
o: All four A, B, AB, O
e: Father passes Iᴬ or Iᴮ while mother always passes i; children can only be Iᴬi (Group A) or Iᴮi (Group B).

q: Two visibly different-looking dogs interbreed and produce healthy fertile puppies. Are they different biological species?
o: No, because members of the same species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring regardless of surface appearance differences
e: Surface trait differences do not create separate species as long as populations freely interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

q: If brown eyes (B) are dominant over blue eyes (b), and both parents are heterozygous brown-eyed (Bb), what is the probability of their child having blue eyes (bb)?
e: From Bb × Bb, genotypes are 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, giving a 1/4 = 25% chance of homozygous recessive blue eyes (bb).

q: Why did Mendel cross-pollinate pure parents (TT × tt) to get F₁, but then allow F₁ plants (Tt) to self-pollinate to get F₂?
o: To test whether the recessive trait hidden in F₁ was truly intact and would segregate and reappear in F₂ without outside pollen
e: Selfing F₁ showed that the recessive allele remained unblended and re-emerged cleanly in 1/4 of the F₂ generation.

q: As early Homo sapiens migrated out of Africa into West Asia, Central Asia, Europe, India, Indonesia and America, what caused local physical differences among populations?
o: Minor adaptive genetic variations to local climates and genetic drift without creating reproductive isolation
e: Dispersing across continents with occasional back-and-forth migration yielded minor superficial differences without forming separate species.

q: Identify the pair that is HOMOLOGOUS (NOT analogous):
o: Human arm and bird wing (forelimb skeleton)
e: Human arm and bird wing both share the fundamental vertebrate forelimb bone pattern inherited from a common tetrapod ancestor (homologous).

q: Why is the fossil Archaeopteryx (with teeth & clawed tail like reptiles, plus feathers & wings like birds) so important in evolution?
o: It shows features of both reptiles and birds, proving birds evolved from reptiles (dinosaurs)
e: Archaeopteryx exhibits both reptilian traits (toothed jaws, bony tail) and avian traits (feathers), linking birds evolutionarily to reptiles.

q: If two heterozygous round-seeded pea plants (Rr × Rr) are crossed and produce 100 seeds, how many are expected to be PURE/homozygous round (RR)?
e: Rr × Rr yields 25% RR (pure round), 50% Rr (hybrid round), and 25% rr (wrinkled). Thus pure RR = 25 seeds.

q: Why can two populations with major differences in chromosome number or DNA no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring?
o: Because germ cells from the two populations cannot fuse successfully or align chromosomes properly to form a viable, fertile offspring
e: Genetic and chromosomal incompatibility prevents successful interbreeding, marking reproductive isolation and completion of speciation.

q: What is common between 50% of human sperms and 100% of human eggs regarding sex chromosomes?
o: Both carry an X sex chromosome (plus 22 autosomes)
e: 100% of eggs (22+X) and 50% of sperms (22+X) carry an X chromosome.

q: What is the ONLY source of new variations in an asexually reproducing population (such as bacteria)?
e: Without gamete fusion from two parents, minor errors during DNA copying are the sole source of variation in asexual reproduction.

q: Which floral feature of pea plants naturally keeps pure lines homozygous unless manually altered by a scientist?
o: Natural self-pollination inside closed bisexual flowers
e: Garden pea flowers naturally self-pollinate to maintain pure lines, while also allowing easy artificial cross-pollination.

q: How does the second method of estimating fossil age work on rocks/fossils scientifically?
o: By detecting the ratios of different isotopes of the same element in the fossil material
e: NCERT states the second method of determining fossil age detects ratios of different isotopes of the same element in fossil material.

q: Once a heritable green colour mutation arises in a beetle population hunted by crows, which mechanism spreads the green trait across generations?
o: Natural selection (green beetles evade predators better, survive and reproduce more green offspring)
e: Since green colour improves survival and reproductive output against predators, natural selection drives its increase.

q: Trait P is inherited from parents to children, whereas Trait Q is NOT. Identify a valid pair (P, Q):
o: P = cut tail, Q = blood group
P = curly hair / attached earlobes, Q = a surgical scar from an accident
P = swimming skill, Q = eye colour
e: Attached/free earlobes and hair texture are inherited traits encoded in germ-cell DNA, while accident scars are non-heritable acquired traits.

Reason (R): Inheritance of seed shape and seed colour occurs independently of each other.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

q:
Assertion (A): Biological evolution is a linear ladder of progress from lower forms to the 'best' ultimate organisms.
Reason (R): Simple ancient bacteria continue to thrive successfully even today in extreme environments like hot springs.

q: Case Study: Mendel crossed pure tall-violet (TTWW) with pure short-white (ttww) pea plants to get all TtWw in F₁. Selfing F₁ gives 320 F₂ plants. How many F₂ plants are expected to be 'Tall with white flowers'?
e: In the 9:3:3:1 ratio, one dominant (Tall) + one recessive (white) trait is 3/16: (3/16) × 320 = 60 plants.

q: Case Study: A woman is unfairly blamed by relatives for giving birth to three consecutive daughters and no son. What is the exact scientific refutation?
o: Mother only contributes an X chromosome in every egg; whether the child is XX (girl) or XY (boy) depends solely on whether the father's sperm carries X or Y
e: All maternal eggs carry X; paternal sperms carry X or Y (50-50), so biologically the father's sperm determines the child's sex.

q: Case Study: Anatomists compare Group I (human arm, dog foreleg, bird wing) and Group II (bat wing, honeybee wing). Which evolutionary concepts do Group I and Group II illustrate respectively?
o: Homologous organs (common ancestor) and Analogous organs (different origin, same function)
e: Group I shares a common vertebrate skeletal blueprint (homologous), while Group II has unrelated origins adapted for flight (analogous).

q: Case Study: On Bush 1, an elephant randomly crushes red beetles sparing only a few blue variants by sheer luck; on Bush 2, green variants camouflage on leaves while crows keep eating red ones. Name the two mechanisms:
o: Case 1: Natural selection; Case 2: Genetic drift
Case 1: Genetic drift (chance); Case 2: Natural selection (adaptation)
e: The elephant accident is genetic drift (random non-adaptive shift), while camouflage against crows is natural selection.

q: Case Study: Excavation shows: Top layer (10 m) — horse/mammal fossils; Middle layer (60 m) — dinosaur fossils; Deepest layer (180 m) — Trilobite/Ammonite fossils. What does this prove?
o: Ancient marine invertebrates appeared earliest, followed by dinosaurs, and later mammals
All arose on the same day
e: Deeper rock layers contain older fossils, confirming marine invertebrates evolved earlier than dinosaurs and mammals.

q: Case Study: Most human populations show free earlobes (dominant) and attached earlobes (recessive). If a homozygous free-earlobed parent (FF) marries an attached-earlobed parent (ff), what will ALL their children have?
e: FF × ff produces 100% heterozygous Ff children, all showing the dominant free earlobe trait.

q: Case Study: Farmers transformed wild cabbage into cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale and kohlrabi. How does this process differ from natural selection?
o: This is 'artificial selection' where humans deliberately breed desired traits, whereas in natural selection environmental factors decide survival
e: In artificial selection, humans select and breed desirable traits purposefully rather than nature selecting traits for survival.

o: X and Y are much more closely related with a much more recent common ancestor than Z
e: Fewer accumulated DNA differences indicate a much more recent divergence from a common ancestor.

q: Case Study: 400 F₂ pea plants are grown from a TT × tt cross. Which distribution matches Mendel's laws accurately?
o: 100 pure tall (TT), 200 hybrid tall (Tt), 100 pure short (tt)
e: 1:2:1 of 400 = 100 TT, 200 Tt, 100 tt (300 tall phenotype, 100 short; pure tall : pure short = 1:1).

q: One TALL pea plant is picked at random from the F₂ generation of a TT × tt cross. What is the probability that this tall plant is heterozygous (Tt)?
e: Careful! Among the TALL phenotype plants in F₂ (1 TT + 2 Tt = 3 total tall plants), 2 out of 3 are heterozygous Tt! Probability = 2/3.

q: What would happen to Mendel's dihybrid 9:3:3:1 ratio if the two genes chosen happened to sit tightly close together on the same chromosome instead of assorting independently?
o: The two genes would tend to be inherited together (linkage), reducing new combinations and deviating from 9:3:3:1
e: Independent assortment giving 9:3:3:1 requires the two traits to segregate independently (e.g. located on separate chromosomes); tight linkage deviates from it.

q: In a boy with XY chromosomes, which parent gave the X chromosome and which parent gave the Y chromosome?
o: X from father, Y from mother
X from the mother (egg) and Y from the father (sperm)
e: A male child always inherits his X chromosome from his mother and his Y chromosome from his father.

q: Why are 'DNA sequence similarity' AND 'homologous forelimb bones' considered two independent yet matching proofs of common ancestry among mammals?
o: Because both macroscopic homologous bone architecture and microscopic DNA sequence similarity independently confirm the same evolutionary tree
e: Anatomical homology, fossil strata and molecular DNA phylogeny converge independently onto the exact same evolutionary tree.

q:
Arrange these 4 events in correct chronological evolutionary order (oldest to newest):
(1) Abiotic amino acid formation & first unicellular life
(2) Trilobites & Ammonites
(3) Feathered dinosaurs & origin of birds
(4) Emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa
e: Sequence: abiotic organic chemistry & first microbes (1) → ancient marine invertebrates (2) → dinosaurs & birds (3) → modern humans (4).

q: Wait: to determine whether a tall pea plant is homozygous (TT) or heterozygous (Tt), what is the BEST single tester plant you should cross it with?
o: With homozygous recessive short (tt)—all tall offspring confirms TT, while 1:1 tall:short confirms Tt
e: A test cross with homozygous recessive (tt) directly reveals the gametes produced by the dominant phenotype individual: 100% tall if TT, 1:1 if Tt.

q: Why are a bird's wing and a human's arm considered homologous even though their external appearance and functions (flying vs grasping) look totally different?
o: Homology is based on shared underlying bone architecture inherited from a common ancestor, not external shape or current function
e: Homology depends on common embryonic/ancestral structural origin rather than superficial appearance or adapted function.

q: Can a variation that provides ZERO survival advantage still become fixed throughout a small isolated population?
o: Yes, through Genetic Drift in a small population, purely by chance even a neutral non-adaptive trait can become fixed
e: Genetic drift causes random changes in allele frequencies in small populations, potentially fixing even neutral traits without natural selection.

q: If intense geological folding flips rock layers upside down so older rocks now lie on top of younger rocks, which fossil dating method still accurately determines absolute age?
o: Radioactive isotope ratio dating inside the fossil itself
e: Isotope dating measures radioactive decay inside the fossil itself, remaining reliable even if tectonic folding disturbs rock layers.

q: Charles Darwin knew evolution occurred via Natural Selection on variations, yet could not explain the mechanism of heredity and variation. Whose laws later supplied the missing genetic mechanism for Darwin's theory?
o: Gregor Mendel's principles of heredity (and later DNA/genetics)
e: Mendel's laws of inheritance (and later DNA/genetics) explained how variations arise and pass down for Darwin's natural selection to act upon.

q: What phenotypic ratio is produced when a heterozygous Round-Yellow pea plant (RrYy) is test-crossed with a homozygous wrinkled-green plant (rryy)?
e: RrYy forms 4 equal gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) combining with ry from rryy to give a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 phenotypic ratio.

q: If both mother and father have blood group AB (genotype IᴬIᴮ), which blood group can NEVER appear in their biological child?
e: Since neither IᴬIᴮ parent carries the recessive 'i' allele, their child can only be A, B or AB—never O (ii).

q: In evolutionary tree relationships, birds and mammals both have 4-chambered hearts, yet evolved separately from reptile ancestors. Does having a 4-chambered heart alone make birds and mammals each other's closest ancestors without considering fossil/DNA history?
o: No, single analogous/convergent traits cannot by themselves establish closest ancestry; overall homologous traits, fossils and DNA determine the evolutionary tree
e: Just as bat and bird wings evolved independently, evolutionary relationships must be built on homologous designs, fossils and DNA comparisons.

q: Mendel combined botany with mathematical/statistical ratios (like 3:1 and 9:3:3:1) over huge sample sizes (~10,000+ pea plants). Why were large sample sizes vital?
o: Small sample sizes deviate randomly by chance, whereas large samples reveal exact underlying genetic ratios cleanly
e: Just as flipping a coin thousands of times eliminates small-sample chance noise, large sample sizes revealed Mendel's exact inheritance ratios.

q: Why was Lamarck's idea of 'inheritance of acquired characters' rejected in favour of Darwin's Natural Selection and Mendelian genetics?
o: Because lifetime somatic modifications do not alter germ-cell DNA; only DNA-encoded traits are inherited while natural selection favoured longer-necked genetic variants
e: Experimental tests and genetics proved somatic experiences cannot rewrite germ-cell DNA; rather, natural selection acts on existing genetic variations.

q: If 5 random beetles from a diverse 10,000-beetle mainland float on a log to a barren island and start a new population, why does the island population often look genetically different from the mainland?
o: Genetic drift (sampling effect in a tiny population), as 5 individuals carry only a random subset of mainland alleles
e: Small founding populations undergo strong genetic drift, drastically shifting trait frequencies compared to the parent mainland population.

q: Across all kingdoms of life (Amoeba, peas, birds, humans), evolutionary change over generations cannot happen without changes in:
o: Heritable DNA (genetic material passed across generations)
e: Evolution requires heritable variation, which ultimately resides in changes to the DNA sequences passed during reproduction.

q: Looking at three pairs: (1) Bird wing & Insect wing, (2) Human tooth & Elephant tusk, (3) Sweet potato & Potato—which pair has the strongest anatomical evidence of a common ancestor?
o: Pair 2 (Human teeth and Elephant tusks — homologous organs)
e: Both human teeth and elephant tusks (modified incisors) share the same basic anatomical origin (homologous), whereas pairs 1 and 3 are analogous.

q: Does being a 'dominant' allele (like having an extra sixth finger, polydactyly, in humans) automatically mean it must be very common in the human population, and a recessive allele must be rare?
o: Yes, dominant is always 75% of population
No! Dominance determines gene expression in a heterozygote, NOT how common an allele is in a large population (which depends on selection and population history)
e: Dominance controls expression inside a single individual (Tt), not allele frequency across a population—for example, blood group O is recessive yet very common globally!

q: Compare Wild Cabbage evolution into Cauliflower vs Dinosaur evolution into Birds:
o: Both operated by selecting from pre-existing genetic variations—driven by human choice (artificial selection) in cabbage and environmental survival (natural selection) in birds
e: Both artificial and natural selection operate by preserving favourable heritable variations across generations—only the selecting agent differs.

q: If a father has blood group A (genotype Iᴬi) and the mother has blood group B (genotype Iᴮi), how many different blood groups are possible among their children?
e: Crossing Iᴬi × Iᴮi yields genotypes IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), and ii (O)—so all 4 blood groups are possible.

q: In the F₂ generation of Mendel's dihybrid cross (RrYy × RrYy), if 1600 seeds are obtained in total, what is the expected combined number of recombinant seeds (Round-Green + Wrinkled-Yellow)?
e: In the 9:3:3:1 ratio, Round-Green (3/16 = 300) and Wrinkled-Yellow (3/16 = 300) sum to 600 recombinant seeds.

q: When a homozygous tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt), what percentage of F₁ offspring will be dwarf (tt)?
e: TT × Tt produces only TT and Tt genotypes (100% tall), so 0% of the progeny will be dwarf.

q: If a bat's wing, a bird's wing, and an insect's (butterfly's) wing are compared together, which analysis of homology and analogy is most accurate?
o: All three are homologous to each other
All three are analogous to each other
Forelimb skeletal plans of bat and bird are homologous, while as flight organs (especially vs insect) they are analogous
Bat and insect wings are homologous
e: Bat and bird forelimbs share a homologous vertebrate bone plan, while their adaptation for flight—especially compared to chitinous insect wings—represents analogy.

q: A geologist finds only invertebrate fossils in deeper rock strata, followed by fish, amphibian, and mammal fossils in progressively upper layers. What does this confirm?
o: Progressive evolution from simpler to more complex organisms occurred over time
e: In relative fossil dating, deeper strata are older than upper strata, demonstrating gradual evolution from simpler to more complex forms.

q: In a small isolated island population, a landslide killed almost all red beetles leaving mainly green beetles behind even though green offered no survival advantage. What is this phenomenon called?
e: Random change in allele frequency in a small population due to chance events without survival advantage is genetic drift.

q: Two sub-populations remain separated by a huge river for hundreds of generations. If the river dries up and individuals from both groups can no longer interbreed, which process is complete?
e: Inability to interbreed after prolonged geographical isolation, drift, and selection marks complete reproductive isolation and speciation.

q: Why is a recessive trait expressed only when both alleles are recessive, and why does each parent contribute only one allele of a gene to the offspring?
o: One dominant allele produces sufficient functional enzyme; meiosis halves chromosome number in gametes
Recessive alleles are destroyed during fertilisation
Only the male parent contributes alleles
e: A single dominant allele encodes enough functional enzyme/protein for phenotype expression, while meiosis ensures each gamete carries one allele.

q: Even after a rat's tail is cut in an accident across 20 generations, all offspring are still born with tails. Which flaw in Lamarck's theory does this expose?
o: Somatic changes cannot be inherited unless they alter the DNA of germ cells
e: Changes in non-reproductive somatic tissues do not modify germ-cell DNA, so acquired traits cannot pass to offspring.

q: What was the major limitation of Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection?
o: How traits are inherited from parents to offspring and the genetic mechanism behind variations
Why beak shapes vary among finches
Why life progressed from simple to complex
e: Lacking knowledge of Mendelian genetics and DNA, Darwin could not explain the mechanism of inheritance or origin of variations.
